title: Implement Min-Heap
description: Array-as-binary-heap with siftUp on push and siftDown on pop — the real priority-queue primitive behind heapsort, Dijkstra, and Top-K.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the contract.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I'm implementing a min-heap class — a priority queue where the smallest element is always accessible at the root. The standard API is `push(x)`, `pop()` returns and removes the min, `peek()` returns the min without removing, and `size()`. Pop on an empty heap — return undefined or throw? I'll assume undefined unless you say otherwise."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Are elements just numbers, or do they have keys/priorities — like `{value, priority}` objects?
• Should the heap be stable — i.e. equal-priority elements come out in insertion order?
• Do you want me to use the array-as-binary-tree representation, or a linked tree of nodes?
• Should `push` and `pop` both be O(log n), or are you OK with some other tradeoff?
sections.why: The stability question is the one most candidates skip — heaps are NOT stable by default, and if the interviewer cares about FIFO-on-tie behavior, you need to add a tiebreaker (typically a monotonic counter as a secondary key). The array-vs-node-tree question matters for code volume: array-backed is the standard interview answer because the index math `(i-1)>>1` / `2i+1` / `2i+2` is what they're testing — a node-tree implementation hides exactly the part they want to see.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name a degenerate priority-queue before reaching for the heap.
sections.say:
"A naive priority queue is just an unsorted array with O(1) push and O(n) pop — scan for the min on every removal. Or flip it: a sorted array with O(n) push (insertion) and O(1) pop. Either way, one of the two ops is linear, which means N operations cost O(n²) in the worst case. For something like 'process a million events by priority,' that's a trillion ops — unacceptable.

"The heap is the trade: both push AND pop become O(log n), so N ops cost O(n log n). And the implementation is *not* a balanced binary search tree — it's much simpler. We exploit the fact that we only ever access the minimum: we don't need the tree fully sorted, just the *heap property* — every node ≤ its children."
sections.why: Two reasons. First, contrasting against the sorted-array and unsorted-array versions teaches the trade explicitly: 'log n on both' is the heap's whole purpose. Second, naming what the heap *doesn't* need — full ordering — sets up the explanation of why it can be array-backed: a fully-ordered structure (BST) needs node pointers because it's irregular; a heap is always a *complete* binary tree, so we can flatten it into an array and address parent/children with arithmetic. That insight is the whole reason the heap is fast in practice.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: Why does the array-as-heap representation work, and what are the invariants?
sections.say:
"Two structural properties together make this work. First, *shape*: a heap is always a complete binary tree — every level full except possibly the last, which fills left-to-right. That lets us number nodes in level order (root=0, then left-to-right by level) and store them contiguously in an array. From any index `i`: parent is `(i - 1) >> 1`, left child is `2*i + 1`, right child is `2*i + 2`. No pointers, no allocations per node — just integer indexing.

"Second, *order*: every parent ≤ both its children (for a min-heap). This is weaker than full sort — siblings can be in any order. That weakness is exactly why insertions and removals only cost log n: we only have to fix one *path* from leaf to root (siftUp on push) or root to leaf (siftDown on pop), and the height of a complete tree of n nodes is `floor(log2(n))`.

"Push: append at the tail (preserves complete shape), then siftUp — swap with parent while parent is larger. Pop: save the root, move the *last* element to index 0 (preserves complete shape), then siftDown — repeatedly swap with the *smaller* child while it's smaller than the current. Both walk one root-to-leaf path, so both are O(log n)."
sections.why: Naming both invariants is what separates the interview answer from a copy-paste implementation. The shape invariant (always complete) is what enables the array representation; the order invariant (parent ≤ children) is what makes the operations log n. Spelling them out *before* writing code lets the interviewer follow your reasoning, and protects against the most common bug — swapping with the *larger* child on siftDown, which leaves the smaller child violating the heap property under it. If you can explain WHY you pick the smaller child, you'll never write that bug.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few operation sequences to confirm the model.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a few sequences to make sure my model is solid." Three sequences cover the load-bearing cases — a mixed push/pop sequence showing siftUp/siftDown, a push-then-drain showing the heap-sort property, and an alternating peek/push showing that peek doesn't mutate.

examples.input: push(5), push(3), push(8), push(1), pop, pop
examples.note: Basic push/pop. Watch the array shape: each push appends and bubbles; each pop swaps last to root and sinks.
examples.trace:
push(5): a=[5]
push(3): a=[5,3] → siftUp: parent(1)=0, a[0]=5>3 → swap → a=[3,5]
push(8): a=[3,5,8] → siftUp: parent(2)=0, a[0]=3<=8 → stop
push(1): a=[3,5,8,1] → siftUp: parent(3)=1, a[1]=5>1 → swap → a=[3,1,8,5] → parent(1)=0, a[0]=3>1 → swap → a=[1,3,8,5]
pop: top=1, last=5, a=[5,3,8] → siftDown: l=1,r=2, smaller=1 (a[1]=3<5) → swap → a=[3,5,8] → l=3 out of bounds → stop. return 1
pop: top=3, last=8, a=[8,5] → siftDown: l=1,r=2 (r oob), smaller=1 (a[1]=5<8) → swap → a=[5,8] → l=3 oob → stop. return 3

examples.note: Heap-sort property: popping repeatedly yields ascending order. This is what makes the heap a priority queue.
examples.trace:
after pushes: a=[1,3,2,5,9,8] (final heap shape)
pop: top=1, last=8 → a=[8,3,2,5,9] → siftDown sinks 8 → a=[2,3,8,5,9]. return 1
pop: top=2, last=9 → a=[9,3,8,5] → siftDown → a=[3,5,8,9]. return 2
pop: top=3, last=9 → a=[9,5,8] → siftDown → a=[5,9,8]. return 3
pop: top=5, last=8 → a=[8,9] → siftDown → a=[8,9]. return 5
pop: top=8, last=9 → a=[9] → empty after pop. return 8
pop: top=9, a=[] → return 9 (no siftDown)
results: [1,2,3,5,8,9] — ascending ✓

examples.input: push(10), peek, push(4), peek, pop, peek
examples.note: Peek doesn't mutate. After pop(4), the heap holds {10} again.
examples.trace:
push(10): a=[10]
peek: a[0]=10 → 10 (no mutation)
push(4): a=[10,4] → siftUp: parent(1)=0, a[0]=10>4 → swap → a=[4,10]
peek: a[0]=4 → 4 (no mutation)
pop: top=4, last=10, a=[10] (no siftDown needed, length 1). return 4
peek: a[0]=10 → 10

sections.why: The first trace surfaces the classic bug: after `last = a.pop()`, you need to check `if (!a.length) return top;` before writing `a[0] = last` — otherwise on a single-element heap you'd assign back the very element you just popped. The second trace defends the heap-sort claim concretely: dump everything, popping in a loop gives ascending order. The third trace defends that peek is a non-mutating read — a surprisingly common bug is implementing peek as 'pop then push back,' which is O(log n) instead of O(1).

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:
• Pop on empty → return undefined (or throw, depending on contract). Decide and document.
• Pop on single-element heap → after `a.pop()`, the array is empty; do NOT then write `a[0] = last` or you'll restore the element you just removed.
• Push of a duplicate → no special handling needed; equal-priority elements coexist in the heap (just not in any guaranteed order between them).
• Equal-priority on siftDown → the `a[l] < a[s]` comparison uses strict `<`, so we don't swap on equality — that's correct (avoids infinite loops) but means stability across equals is NOT guaranteed.
• Numeric vs object comparison → if elements are objects with a priority field, you need a comparator parameter; the canonical assumes raw numbers and the `<=` / `<` operators work directly.
• Very large heaps → log n grows slowly; even a billion elements is only ~30 levels. The array can hit GC pressure but the algorithm doesn't."
sections.why: The 'empty after pop' edge is the one that crashes implementations under test — `a.pop()` on a length-1 array leaves length 0, and writing `a[0] = last` silently revives it. The 'equality = no swap' edge defends correctness (avoids infinite swap loops on equal siblings) but also calls out a real-world tradeoff: if you need stable priority-queue semantics (FIFO on ties), you have to add a monotonic counter as a secondary key. Mentioning that unprompted is the senior-tier signal.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time: push and pop are both O(log n) — each walks one root-to-leaf path of a complete binary tree, and the height of a complete binary tree of n nodes is ⌊log₂ n⌋. Peek and size are O(1). Building a heap from n existing elements by calling push n times is O(n log n), BUT there's a clever trick — `heapify` — that builds a heap in O(n) by sift-down-ing from the middle of the array backward. Worth mentioning if asked.

"Space: O(n) for the backing array, O(1) per operation.

"If you wanted me to extend this: a max-heap is the same code with `<=` flipped to `>=` and the smaller-child pick flipped to larger. A priority queue with key/value pairs swaps the raw comparison for a comparator callback. And this is the building block for heapsort (push everything, pop everything, you get O(n log n) sorting), Dijkstra's shortest-path (PQ keyed by distance), A* search, top-K problems, and Median-of-Stream — they all sit on top of this one primitive."
sections.why: The amortized defense for heap is the cleanest of any common data structure: 'complete binary tree, height log n, each op walks one path.' No subtleties. The bonus material — heapify-in-O(n), max-heap variant, downstream uses — is what proves you see this as a *foundation*, not a one-off. Naming heapsort, Dijkstra, and Median-of-Stream unprompted shows you understand the heap's role in the broader algorithmic toolbox.

walkthrough.intro: Step through a sequence of MinHeap operations. Each example is a list of method calls; the state panel shows the backing array `a` (in heap-array form — root at index 0, children at 2i+1 and 2i+2). Every peek / pop result is collected into a `results` array so you can verify pops come out in ascending order.

notes: Push: append at the end, then siftUp — swap with parent while parent is larger.
Pop: save root, move last element to index 0, then siftDown — swap with the SMALLER child while it is smaller.
Always swap with the smaller child on siftDown — swapping with the larger one would violate the heap property.
reference.crux: Store the complete tree in a flat array — parent=(i-1)>>1, children=2i+1/2i+2 — so push/pop only fix ONE root-to-leaf path by sifting, giving O(log n).
cruxDistractors: Keep the backing array fully sorted on every push so the min is always at index 0 — but insertion is then O(n).
Use a self-balancing BST of nodes; the leftmost node is the min, and rotations keep it O(log n).
On siftDown, swap with the LARGER child while it exceeds the current node, walking down until the heap settles.

alternates.label: Bottom-up heapify constructor (Floyd's O(n) build)
alternates.when: Reach for this when the interviewer hands you an existing array and asks you to heapify it in place — pushing n items one-by-one is O(n log n), but Floyd's bottom-up siftDown builds the heap in O(n). The intuition: most nodes are near the bottom (n/2 leaves need no work; the next level needs at most 1 swap each), so the total work telescopes to O(n) by the standard sum Σ(h · n/2^(h+1)) = 2n.
notes: Start siftDown from index `(n>>1) - 1` — the last internal node. Indices past that are leaves: a single-node subtree is already a valid heap, so they need no work.
The O(n) bound is non-obvious: it's NOT n/2 · log n. Most nodes are near the bottom (cheap to sift), and the sum Σ(h · n/2^(h+1)) collapses to 2n by the geometric-series identity.
Push and pop still cost O(log n) — bottom-up heapify only speeds up the INITIAL build from a known array, not subsequent operations.

questions.q: Given index i, the parent index is:
On siftDown, which child do you swap with when both children are smaller than the node?
options: The smaller of the two children
questions.explain: Swapping with the larger child would leave the smaller child violating the heap property under it.

questions.q: Time complexity of push and pop?
Why move the LAST element to index 0 before siftDown on pop?
options: The last element is guaranteed to be the second-smallest, so it is the cheapest replacement for the root
It keeps the underlying array contiguous so the tree shape stays complete
It promotes the deepest leaf, which is closest to becoming the new root after siftDown
siftDown only restores order downward — without seeding index 0 from the tail, the loop has no starting node

exercises.prompt: Fill in the MinHeap. Index math and the smaller-child pick are the load-bearing blanks.

L3.prompt: Implement a MinHeap class with push, pop, peek, and size. Push 5,3,8,1,9,2 then pop everything into an array and log `JSON.stringify` of it.
hints: Push: append at tail, then siftUp by comparing to parent at (i-1)>>1.
Pop: save a[0], move the last element to index 0, then siftDown picking the SMALLER child while it is smaller.
Popping in a loop yields ascending order — that is the heap-sort principle.
